note: The Dorian 6th aimed for over the two-chord Dorian vamp: a solo-over that rings the root on the 1st chord and the 6th (the 3rd of the 4th chord) on the change, then longer phrases over the backing track with two neighbouring positions on the neck. The key is moves (any key), so chords are chord tokens counted the long way once, the title names the key as {{=key}}, and a {{?key}} line says what stays the same. Folds in the Dm7-and-G7 version of the same drill.

exercise.title: {{=key}} Dorian: solo over {{chord:i7}} and {{chord:IV7}}
exercise.why: The 6th of the Dorian scale is the 3rd of the chord built on its 4th note, so landing on it as that chord arrives makes one note say both the mode and the chord.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the backing track. It switches between {{chord:i7}}, the 1st chord of the key, built on {{1}}, and {{chord:IV7}}, the 4th chord, built on {{4}}.
Improvise with the dots of the {{=key}} Dorian scale on the neck. Land on {{1}} when {{chord:i7}} comes round and on {{6}} when {{chord:IV7}} comes round: the ringed note shows the one to aim for.
Practice until your phrase reaches {{6}} on the first beat of the change, not after it.

Press Play below to start the backing track: drums, bass and keys on the same two chords. Under it are positions 1 and 2 of the {{=key}} Dorian scale, with {{1}} and {{6}} ringed. Play longer phrases now, and put {{6}} somewhere in each one: on the change, held, or passed through quickly.
If you lose the chords, stop on a ringed {{1}} and wait for {{chord:i7}} to come round.
{{?key}}In another key both positions sit on other frets, and {{6}} is still the 3rd of {{chord:IV7}}.
